doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Brookmeyer's advice to delay the solo
summary: Rowe cites Bob Brookmeyer on putting off the solo; Israels finds Brookmeyer full of dichotomies but sees the compositional point.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I’m reminded of a quote, Dave Rivello, who is at Eastman School of Music, attributed to Bob Brookmeyer. And he said, “When you write a big band arrangement try to put off as long as you can the solo.”
Oh well, it depends. I mean I guess, maybe.

It’s a challenge you know, because we say okay we have an intro, then we do the head, whatever it is, and we’ll do the bridge. And if you’re A-A-B-A, and then you get to that spot, now I have a shout chorus in mind, but I can’t do it yet.

Yeah maybe, yeah. I also, I understand his position about that. I find Bobby Brookmeyer a kind of a difficult person because he’s full of dichotomies. He has done extraordinarily beautiful work and some obtuse stuff that I just don’t understand at all.

I don’t know what the development of his aesthetics, what he went through, but nevertheless I think he’s been a thoughtful person about these things and there are some — something in what he’s saying there is don’t take the easy way out and just give it to the soloist, now, develop your piece further. And I think that’s, as a composer, that’s a valid perception, a valid goal.
